enonce_markdown: The colonists protested against the Stamp Act of 1765 mainly on the ground that:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Colonial protests of the 1760s were first of all about constitutional principle: who had the right to impose taxes. Identify the principle behind the slogan 'no taxation without representation'.

### Solution

The Stamp Act was an internal tax on printed matter voted by the British Parliament, where the colonists had no elected members. They argued that only their own assemblies could tax them. The amount of the tax was small, the Act did not forbid inter-colonial trade, and it had nothing to do with the Church of England. The correct option is therefore the one about taxation without representation.

choix.texte: the rate of the tax was higher than the rate paid by people living in Britain
the money raised was to be spent only on the Church of England in America
Parliament, in which they had no elected representatives, had no right to tax them
the Act forbade trade between one colony and another

enonce_markdown: The Coercive (Intolerable) Acts were passed by the British Parliament in 1774. State two measures contained in these Acts and say what event they were a response to.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Link each measure to its cause: in an answer on the Revolution, name the Act or measure, then say what it changed for the colonists.

### Solution

They were a response to the Boston Tea Party of December 1773, when colonists destroyed East India Company tea. Two measures: (1) the Boston Port Act closed the port of Boston to trade until the destroyed tea was paid for; (2) the Massachusetts Government Act reduced self-government in Massachusetts (the council was appointed by the Crown and town meetings were restricted). Other measures: the Administration of Justice Act (certain trials moved out of the colony) and a new Quartering Act (troops housed by the colonists).

enonce_markdown: The Declaration of Independence (4 July 1776) justified the break with Britain mainly by arguing that:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A founding document justifies action with a political theory. Identify the Enlightenment idea (John Locke's social contract) behind the text before checking the options.

### Solution

The Declaration states that people have natural rights, that governments get their just power from the consent of the governed, and that when a government destroys those rights the people may alter or abolish it. It then lists George III's wrongs as proof of tyranny. Divine right of kings and the sovereignty of Parliament are the opposite arguments, used by the British side, and mercantilism is an economic system, not a justification for revolt.

choix.texte: government rests on the consent of the governed, who may change it when it violates their natural rights
the king ruled by divine right and could be removed only by the Church
Parliament was sovereign over every part of the empire and could be resisted only by force
the mercantilist system gave each colony the right to leave once it had become rich

enonce_markdown: The American victory at Saratoga (October 1777) was a turning point in the war chiefly because:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

To judge a turning point, ask what it changed afterwards, not only who won the battle.

### Solution

General Burgoyne's army surrendered at Saratoga. The result convinced France, which wanted revenge for 1763, that the Americans could win, and in February 1778 France signed a treaty of alliance with the United States, bringing money, ships and troops. The war did not end at Saratoga (it ended militarily at Yorktown in 1781), New York stayed in British hands, and Britain recognised independence only in 1783.

choix.texte: it forced Britain to recognise American independence at once
it gave Washington control of New York City
it ended British naval power in the Atlantic
it led France to ally openly with the United States in 1778

enonce_markdown: Explain why the Quebec Act of 1774 alarmed many colonists in the Thirteen Colonies.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In a short explanation, give the provisions of the measure first, then the colonists' reading of them, then the link with the wider crisis.

### Solution

The Act enlarged the province of Quebec to the Ohio River, kept French civil law and gave freedom of worship to Roman Catholics. Colonists with land claims in the west saw their expansion blocked. Protestant colonists feared Catholic influence and a government without an elected assembly. Because it was passed at the same time as the Coercive Acts, it was counted among the 'Intolerable Acts' and seen as proof of a British plan to restrict colonial liberties, which pushed the colonies towards the First Continental Congress (September 1774).

enonce_markdown: Historians who link the Revolution to the end of the Seven Years' War (1763) argue that:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Evaluate a causal claim by checking whether each option states a link between the 1763 settlement and the later quarrel, and whether the facts in it are right.

### Solution

After 1763 Britain had a very large war debt and a larger empire to defend, so London looked for revenue in the colonies (Sugar Act, Stamp Act). At the same time the removal of the French from Canada reduced colonial need for British protection. The Proclamation of 1763, which closed the land west of the Appalachians to settlement, added to the anger. The other options are false: Britain won the war, it did not lose its ability to enforce laws, it never gave the colonies seats in Parliament, and the Proclamation restricted western settlement.

choix.texte: Britain's defeat in the war left it too weak to enforce any law in the colonies
the removal of the French threat reduced colonial need for British protection while war debts led London to raise revenue in America
the Treaty of Paris gave the colonists free settlement of all land west of the Mississippi
Britain offered seats in Parliament to the colonies to share the war debt, and they refused
